Ignore people that say you can just install Cinnamon in Ubuntu. You can, but it's definitely not the same. And by the time you got the system to a place it was the same (which would take time/effort/research), you'd pretty much have Linux Mint anyway. Mint also has less of a load than Ubuntu, which is why many people prefer it, especially for older hardware.

 

I know Mint shares some of the features of Ubuntu as well as Debian.

You can also take a look at LMDE (Linux Mint Debian Edition). While Linux Mint is built on top of Ubuntu which is built on top of Debian. LMDE skips building on top of Ubuntu and goes straight for the Debian.

In Essence Debian -> Ubuntu -> Linux Mint Debian -> Linux Mint Debian Edition

Why would you pick LMDE over Mint? It cuts out the middle man.

 

Now the middle man in this case is Canonical, so you lose out on the modifications they are doing to the base Debian system. This is actually preferred by many people, however, because now...

Less Bloat - Faster load times, and less ram in use.

Rolling Release - You don't have to install Linux Mint 18 over Linux Mint 17 when it's released. The release is "rolling", meaning constantly moving forward/updating through the package manager.

However, Unless you want to learn LMDE, I'd advise against it. The gainz are minimal, and honestly it's more of a super-nerd-fetish system. It's not compatible with PPAs, and has a smaller userbase (meaning harder to get help when you need).

 

TL/DR If you want something that simply works, and is beautiful, and has a good user base, and a proven track record. Get Linux Mint

If you want headaches and to spend weeks on trivial problems that will increase your inner nerd. Get testing

It's pretty damned easy. Can't recommend Mint enough. Specifically the MATE version. Just a beautiful, easy to use and fast OS all around. I prefer the Debian edition, which is even faster and more stable, but that may limit gaming for you if you're into that. Some of the Ubuntu PPAs (that work in stock Mint, but not LMDE) available are convenient if you're a gamer.

If you keep /home in a separate partition, you can change distros and keep things like your user settings for applications. I have reinstalled Gentoo and even switched distros a few times with a separate /home partition, and even things like my KDE settings stay in tact (provided all the widgets I installed get re-installed). You should be able to move /home to a new partition even if you haven't already without need to reinstall. I would consult a guide online and ask someone, even me, if it's a good way to do it.

However I think you're jumping the gun. There's no reason to switch from a Debian based distro to another Debian based distribution like you're saying you want to do. It will still use systemd, apt, etc. Basically, all the same lower level packages (AFAIK, I have used Gentoo for years now).

When I was staring out with Linux, I basically just installed all the DEs that looked appealing to me and then chose which one I liked the most. You can change from the login manager (but it seems like you already know this). You can do that for now. The main difference between distributions are things like package mangers and init systems. Most distributions are extremely similar to exiting ones, they just change default installed applications and DE. Sometimes you get custom DEs but that's rare when you consider just how many distributions exist.

Distribution switches are usually reserved for big changes. I switched to Gentoo because I have AMD hardware that's usually not targeted by compilers for performance, to avoid systemd and pulse audio, and for performance related reasons due to work. Generally, re-installing and going through that huge mess of setting up everything you have set up is not worth it just to try different DEs.

And apt is a very good package manager IMO. I think it's second best next to Gentoo Portage and Emerge, but only because Gentoo's tools are so versatile that nothing that relies on binary packages can come close. Gentoo, if you're not aware, compiles almost all software from source code (unless source isn't available). So you can customize your whole OS and decide what you want to use. The downside is it has long compile times, even on higher end hardware. But the trade off to some people is worth it, because you basically choose your own everything and create your own custom distribution. For example, I run with KDE, no systemd, no pulse audio. I don't know a lot of distributions that are overly mainstream that give you that option. But in Gentoo, it's just a matter of changing use flags in a text file.

Something like Gentoo is why you should switch distributions, for those reasons. Installing an entirely different DE is really easy in Linux. It's not like Windows where the whole OS is tied to Aero in win7 or Metro in win8. You can do whatever you want in Linux because it's so modular. I have seen quite a few people new to Linux or trying to understand it having a difficult time grasping the concept that the entire desktop environment and graphical interface is completely decoupled from the OS and can be switched at will.

Mint is just a spin of Ubuntu. To switch, you don't even need to re-install. You just need to change your /etc/apt/sources.list.

Switching from Debian (and by extension, LMDE) to Ubuntu is just as easy. Ubuntu applies its own patches to selected parts of the Debian sources and increases the version. Switching from Ubuntu to Debian is less trivial. I've done both.

Switching to a different distribution entirely, such as Slackware or Gentoo or SuSE, does require a re-install of the base system. You can keep your /home, but if the new distribution uses older versions of your software than the previous one, some applications may not work anymore, so it is a good idea to back up your settings, or create a new user just for testing purposes.

pretty much all distros should have support for making a separate "home" partition. you might need to manually partition but that'll make switching distros much easier. you can just remove all hidden files from your home folder, delete the system partitions for your old distro, and install a new distro, making sure you point it to the existing home folder.

this way all your files are preserved, although installed programs and settings won't.
